posts.author: Family Ministries
posts.seoTitle: Family Devotions at Dinner: 5 Ways to Build Faith
posts.metaDesc: Simple family devotion ideas for dinner: share a blessing, pray for a neighbor by name, read one verse and ask the youngest, and more, rooted in Scripture.
posts.excerpt: Faith grows at home through small moments repeated often, and five simple habits can turn your dinner table into a place where children meet God.
body: The plates are on the table, someone is already reaching for the rice, a phone buzzes, and a child is telling a story about school that has no clear ending. It is not exactly a quiet, holy scene. Yet for many families, this messy moment is the one time each day when everyone is in the same room. That makes the dinner table one of the most important places in the home.

Many parents feel a quiet guilt about family worship. They imagine a long, structured devotional with songs, a lesson, and children sitting perfectly still, and when that feels out of reach, it is easy to do nothing. The Bible paints a much simpler and more hopeful picture of how faith passes from one generation to the next.

This article offers five small, repeatable ways to build faith at the dinner table. None takes more than a few minutes or requires perfect children. What they require is something every family can give: consistency, honesty, and a willingness to let God into the rhythm of a meal.
## The short answer
[[stats]] 5 | Simple habits for any family table || 5 minutes | Is often enough to begin || 1 verse | Can shape a whole conversation

Faith grows at home most naturally through small moments repeated often, not through rare, impressive events. Scripture calls parents to talk about God's words "when thou sittest in thine house" (Deuteronomy 6:7), and few places capture sitting in the house better than the family table. Five simple practices can turn that table into a place of worship: sharing a blessing, praying for a neighbor by name, reading one verse and asking the youngest, telling stories of God's faithfulness, and making room for guests.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church teaches in Fundamental Belief 23 that parents are to bring up their children to love and obey the Lord. The Adventist Department of Family Ministries describes family worship not as something to force on anyone, but as an opportunity to strengthen relationships with one another and with God. That is exactly the spirit of these five ideas.
## Why the table matters so much

When God gave Israel His words through Moses, He did not tell parents to save faith for the temple or for special occasions. He placed it right in the middle of daily life. The words are simple enough for any parent to understand.

> "And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Deuteronomy 6:6 to 7, KJV

Notice the order. The words must first be "in thine heart" before they can be taught, because children learn more from what we love than from what we say. Then notice the setting: sitting, walking, lying down, rising up. God built the passing on of faith into the most ordinary moments of family life, and mealtime is one of the clearest.

Jesus often revealed God's love around a table. After His resurrection, two discouraged disciples recognized Him only when He sat at meat with them and "took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him" (Luke 24:30 to 31). The early church also met "breaking bread from house to house" (Acts 2:46). The table has always been a place where people meet Jesus.

[[callout]] What makes table faith work || Short and simple beats long and rare || Consistency matters more than perfection || Let children participate, not just listen || Keep it warm, never forced or used as punishment
## Five ways to build faith at the dinner table
### 1. Share a blessing before you eat

The simplest place to begin is with thanks. Before the first bite, pause together and thank God for the food and for one another. Jesus modeled this when He "had given thanks" before distributing the loaves (John 6:11), and Paul encourages us, "In every thing give thanks" (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

To make the blessing more than a routine, invite each person to name one specific thing they are thankful for that day. A child might name sunshine at recess, and a parent might be grateful simply that everyone is home. Over time, this trains the whole family to notice God's goodness, echoing the psalmist: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits" (Psalm 103:2).

In many Haitian homes, blessing the food is already a cherished habit, sometimes prayed in Kreyòl by a grandparent. If that is part of your family story, keep it alive. Let the children hear the prayers of the older generation, and let them pray in the language of their heart too.
### 2. Pray for a neighbor by name

Faith grows when it looks outward. A powerful habit is to pray together for one specific person outside the home, by name. It might be a neighbor down the street, a classmate who seems lonely, a coworker going through a hard time, or a relative back in Haiti.

Scripture calls us to pray for others. Paul urged that "supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men" (1 Timothy 2:1). When God's people were living as exiles far from home, He told them to "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it" (Jeremiah 29:7). That verse can speak especially to immigrant families who are learning to love a new community while still carrying their homeland in their hearts.

Praying by name helps children understand that prayer is a real conversation with a God who cares about real people. It also opens the door to action. A family that prays for a lonely neighbor on Monday might bake bread for that neighbor on Thursday.

[[steps]] Choose | Pick one person outside your home to pray for this week || Name | Say their name aloud in prayer at dinner || Notice | Ask each other what that person might need || Act | Find one small way to show them kindness || Follow up | Share what happened at a later meal
### 3. Read one verse and ask the youngest

Family Bible reading does not need to be long to be meaningful. Choose one short verse, read it aloud, and then ask the youngest person at the table a simple question about it. What do you think this means? Who in this verse needs help? What does this tell us about God?

Starting with the youngest keeps the conversation simple, shows little ones their thoughts matter, and invites older family members to listen instead of lecture. Jesus said, "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:14). Sometimes a four year old's simple answer opens a deeper conversation than any adult could plan.

Scripture also expects children to ask questions about faith. Moses wrote, "And when thy son asketh thee in time to come, saying, What mean the testimonies, and the statutes, and the judgments" (Deuteronomy 6:20), and then told parents to answer with the story of how God saved them. Questions are not a threat to faith. They are an invitation to share it.
[[table]] Verse to read | A question for the youngest
[[table]] Psalm 119:105 | What does a lamp help us do in the dark?
[[table]] John 6:35 | Why do you think Jesus called Himself bread?
[[table]] Psalm 23:2 | Where is your favorite peaceful place?
[[table]] Proverbs 15:17 | What makes a meal feel full of love?
[[table]] 1 Peter 5:7 | What is one worry you can give to God tonight?
![A book and a cup resting on a quiet table](1646248340253-68514f8d4b77)
### 4. Tell stories of God's faithfulness

Every family has stories of times when God provided, protected, or answered prayer. These stories are some of the most precious things a family can pass down. Scripture says, "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done" (Psalm 78:4).

Once a week or so, invite someone to share a story: how grandparents came to know Jesus, how the family found its way to a new country, or a time when money was short and God made a way. Keep the stories honest and short. Children who hear them begin to see their own lives as part of a bigger story God is writing.

Many Haitian families carry rich stories of faith through hardship, migration, and new beginnings. Telling those stories honestly, including the hard parts, helps children understand that faith is not pretending life is easy. It is trusting God in the middle of real life. Even the prophet Joel, describing a devastating locust plague, told the people, "Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation" (Joel 1:3), because the hard chapters belong in the story too.
### 5. Make room for others at your table

The final way to build faith at the table is to open it. Inviting a guest, whether a neighbor, a new friend from church, a lonely student, or a family new to the area, teaches children that God's love is meant to be shared. Paul encouraged believers to be "given to hospitality" (Romans 12:13), and the early church grew around open homes and shared meals.

Hospitality does not require a fancy meal, and a simple pot of rice and beans served with warmth can be a meaningful gift. Proverbs reminds us, "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" (Proverbs 15:17). What guests remember is not the menu but the welcome.

At Shekinah in Alvarado, the church family shares a meal together after the Sabbath service, and visitors are welcome at the table. The Sabbath table at church and the dinner table at home can strengthen one another. Children who see the same welcome and faith in both places learn that hospitality is part of following Jesus.
![A table set with plates of fresh, colorful food ready to share](1547573854-74d2a71d0826)
## Proverbs 22:6 and the long view

Many parents hold onto a familiar promise: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it" (Proverbs 22:6). Proverbs are general principles of how life usually works under God's blessing, not guarantees that override a child's free choice. Even faithful parents sometimes watch a child wander.

What this verse does promise is that training matters. The small, repeated habits of childhood leave deep marks that often remain long after a child has grown up. A prayer heard a thousand times at the dinner table, a verse discussed over rice and beans, or a story of God's faithfulness told on a hard night can become a lifeline years later. Our role is to plant faithfully and to trust God with the harvest.
[[link]] Diri ak Pwa the Healthy Way | /blog/diri-ak-pwa-the-healthy-way/
## Getting started this week

You do not need to begin with all five habits at once, which can make family worship feel heavy. Choose one practice, perhaps the shared blessing, and do it every evening this week. When it feels natural, add a second.

Keep the tone warm and light. If a child is restless, keep it short, and if you miss a night, simply begin again. The goal is not a perfect program but a home where God is a natural part of the conversation and faith belongs at the table as surely as food does.
## Reflection questions

Take a moment to think about your own family table. What does a typical meal in your home feel like right now, and where might there be space for even one minute of faith? Which of these five habits feels most natural for your family to begin this week? And what story of God's faithfulness from your own life would you most want your children or grandchildren to remember?
## A word of encouragement

If you feel like you have fallen short as a parent or grandparent, please hear this. God does not ask for perfect families. He asks for willing hearts. The same Jesus who welcomed restless children and broke bread with discouraged disciples is glad to sit at your table too, noise and spilled cups included.

Every small moment of faith you share is a seed, and some take years to sprout. None of them are wasted in God's hands. Keep showing up, keep praying, and trust Him to do what only He can do in the hearts of the people you love.
## A prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the gift of family and for the food on our table. Come and sit with us at every meal. Help us to give thanks, to pray for our neighbors, to listen to our children, and to tell the stories of Your goodness. Where we feel tired or unsure, give us patience and joy. Let our home be a place where everyone who sits at our table can taste and see that You are good. Amen.
## Your next step

If you would like help building faith in your home, a free Bible study is a wonderful place to start, for yourself or together as a family. Request one below and study at your own pace with someone who cares. And if you are near Alvarado, we would love to welcome your family on Sabbath morning at 205 E Carver St and invite you to stay for our shared meal.

posts.excerpt: A simple guide to healthy Haitian inspired plant based meals, the Adventist health message, and a fresh mango and avocado salad you can make in fifteen minutes.
body: It is Thursday evening, the week has been long, and you are standing in front of an open refrigerator hoping dinner will plan itself. You want to eat better, maybe because a doctor mentioned your blood pressure or maybe because you simply feel tired more than you used to. But every healthy recipe you find online seems to call for ingredients you have never heard of, and none of it tastes like home. If you grew up with diri ak pwa on the table and the smell of epis in the kitchen, you may wonder whether eating well means leaving your culture behind.

Here is some good news. Many Haitian dishes are already built on beans, rice, vegetables, fruit, herbs, and spices. With a few simple changes, such as choosing brown rice, adding more vegetables, and using less salt and oil, a traditional Haitian plate can become deeply nourishing. You do not need an expensive diet plan, and you do not need to stop enjoying your food.

In this guide we will look at what the Bible says about food, why Seventh-day Adventists encourage a plant based way of eating, and what researchers have learned from Adventists in Loma Linda, California. Then we will build a simple weekly plate and finish with a bright mango and avocado salad.
## The short answer

A healthy plant based Haitian meal is simple: fill half your plate with vegetables and fruit, a quarter with a whole grain like brown rice, and a quarter with beans or another plant protein, then season it the way your grandmother would with epis, thyme, garlic, and lime. Harvard's Healthy Eating Plate uses this same basic shape, recommending that half the plate be vegetables and fruits, a quarter whole grains, and a quarter protein, with healthy plant oils in moderation and water to drink.
[[stats]] 73,308 | Adventists followed in a 2013 JAMA Internal Medicine study || 12% | Fewer deaths among vegetarians over about six years || 1/2 | Of the plate for vegetables and fruits

For Seventh-day Adventists, this is about more than lab numbers. It flows from a conviction that our bodies belong to God and that caring for them is part of worship. Food is one way we thank the Creator every day.
## What the Bible says about food and health
### God's first menu
The very first conversation about food in Scripture happens in the Garden of Eden, before sin had entered the world. God set before Adam and Eve a table full of plants, seeds, and fruit.

> "And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat." Genesis 1:29, KJV

In the King James Version, "meat" simply means food. The Bible directly tells us that God's original diet for humanity was made of plants. After the Flood God permitted people to eat meat (Genesis 9:3), and Scripture distinguishes between clean and unclean animals (Leviticus 11). For this reason the Adventist Church encourages a vegetarian diet but does not teach that eating clean meat is a sin, while it does ask members to abstain from the unclean meats identified in Leviticus 11 (Fundamental Belief 22). What many Adventists draw from Genesis 1:29 is an interpretation and an invitation: the closer we come to God's original plan, the more we may enjoy the health He intended.
### Your body is a temple
Paul wrote to believers in Corinth who acted as if what they did with their bodies had nothing to do with their faith. His answer was direct and personal.

> "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's." 1 Corinthians 6:19 to 20, KJV

Paul's main concern in that passage was sexual purity, but the principle reaches every part of life. If Jesus paid for us with His own life, then our bodies are not cheap. Feeding them well is one small, daily way of honoring the price He paid.
### God cares about your whole life

The apostle John opened a short letter to his friend Gaius with a warm blessing: "Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth" (3 John 1:2). God is not only interested in our souls. He cares about our energy, our sleep, our strength, and the food on our plates, because He cares about us as whole people.
## The Adventist health message

Seventh-day Adventists have taught healthy living since the church's earliest days. Fundamental Belief 22, on Christian Behavior, says that "because our bodies are the temples of the Holy Spirit, we are to care for them intelligently," and that "we are to adopt the most healthful diet possible and abstain from the unclean foods identified in the Scriptures." The same belief asks members to abstain from alcohol, tobacco, and the irresponsible use of drugs.

On its official health page, the Adventist Church describes a well balanced vegetarian diet that includes legumes, whole grains, nuts, fruits, and vegetables, along with a source of vitamin B12. That last detail matters. The National Institutes of Health notes that plant foods have no vitamin B12 unless they are fortified, and that people who eat little or no animal foods might not get enough. Fortified foods, such as some breakfast cereals and nutritional yeasts, or a supplement can help fill that gap. Talk with your doctor about what is right for you, especially if you are pregnant, nursing, or managing a health condition.
## What researchers learned from Loma Linda

Loma Linda, California, is home to a large community of Seventh-day Adventists and to Loma Linda University, an Adventist institution. Researchers there have been studying the health of Adventists for decades through the Adventist Health Studies. The current study, Adventist Health Study 2, includes more than 96,000 church members from the United States and Canada.

In 2013, a team led by Dr. Michael Orlich published findings from 73,308 Adventists in the journal JAMA Internal Medicine. Over roughly six years, vegetarians in the study had 12 percent fewer deaths than those who ate meat regularly. The study included vegans, lacto ovo vegetarians, people who ate fish but no other meat, and people who ate meat only occasionally. The study also benefited from the fact that Adventists tend to drink little alcohol and rarely smoke, which makes it easier to see the effect of diet itself.

Loma Linda is also one of the places featured in the Blue Zones project, which studies communities where people tend to live long lives. The Blue Zones website says Adventists in Loma Linda live as much as a decade longer than other Americans, and points to a plant rich diet, nuts, regular moderate exercise, close friendships, and the weekly Sabbath rest. Research like this does not prove that any single food will add years to your life, but it paints a picture of a faithful, balanced lifestyle.
[[link]] The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship | /blog/the-gift-of-rest-why-sleep-is-part-of-our-worship/
## Building a Haitian plate the healthy way

You do not need to invent a new cuisine. You only need to tilt the plate you already love toward more plants. Harvard nutrition researchers point out that no single fruit or vegetable provides every nutrient we need, and that variety matters as much as quantity. They also note that potatoes do not count toward the vegetable half of the plate, because they are starchy and digest quickly.

[[callout]] Four simple swaps || Choose brown rice for diri ak pwa instead of white rice || Make legim with extra eggplant, cabbage, chayote, and spinach || Cook beans from dry and season with epis instead of salty cubes || Add fresh fruit like mango or a slice of zaboka to the plate
### Diri ak pwa with brown rice

Rice and beans are the heart of many Haitian meals. Brown rice keeps the bran and germ of the grain, which hold much of its fiber, and the beans bring protein and fiber of their own. We walk through the full recipe in our article on diri ak pwa the healthy way.
### Legim full of vegetables

Legim is a thick Haitian vegetable stew, usually made with mashed eggplant, cabbage, chayote, spinach, and other vegetables, flavored with epis, onion, garlic, and tomato paste. It is sometimes cooked with meat, but it is wonderful on its own, and the vegetables are the true stars of the dish anyway. Spoon it over brown rice, add a side of black beans, and you have a deeply Haitian, fully plant based meal.
### Fruit, avocado, and fresh salads

Avocado, called zaboka in Kreyòl, is a familiar and beloved part of the Haitian plate next to rice and beans. A fresh salad with mango, avocado, tomato, and lime brings color and brightness to heavier dishes. It is also an easy way to add more fruit and vegetables.
![Sliced mango and avocado arranged together on a plate](1417217601328-d3c66e6f1d48)
## A simple weekly plate idea

Here is one way to plan a week of plant based Haitian inspired dinners. Treat it as a starting point, not a rule. Cook a large pot of beans and a pot of brown rice early in the week, and several meals are already half done.
[[table]] Day | Plant based plate idea
[[table]] Sunday | Diri ak pwa with brown rice, steamed greens, sliced avocado
[[table]] Monday | Legim over brown rice with a side of black beans
[[table]] Tuesday | Leftover diri ak pwa with mango avocado salad
[[table]] Wednesday | Bean and vegetable soup with whole grain bread
[[table]] Thursday | Boiled plantain, sòs pwa, and a cabbage and carrot salad
[[table]] Friday | Soup joumou, plant based, with chickpeas
[[table]] Sabbath | A make ahead meal from Friday, such as legim, rice, and fresh fruit

Friday cooking matters for many Adventist families, because preparing meals ahead lets the whole household rest and enjoy the Sabbath without spending hours in the kitchen. A pot of legim or soup tastes even better the next day, which makes it a natural Sabbath dish.
## Featured recipe: Salad mango ak zaboka

This mango and avocado salad is bright, cool, and ready in about fifteen minutes. It works beside a warm plate of diri ak pwa, and with a can of black beans stirred in, it becomes a light lunch of its own. It serves four as a side dish.
[[table]] Ingredient | Amount
[[table]] Ripe mangoes, peeled and diced | 2 medium (about 2 cups)
[[table]] Ripe avocados, diced | 2 medium
[[table]] Cherry tomatoes, halved | 1 cup
[[table]] Cucumber, diced | 1 small
[[table]] Red onion, finely chopped | 1/4 cup
[[table]] Fresh parsley or cilantro, chopped | 1/4 cup
[[table]] Fresh lime juice | 3 tablespoons (about 2 limes)
[[table]] Olive oil | 1 tablespoon
[[table]] Salt | 1/4 teaspoon, or to taste
[[table]] Scotch bonnet pepper, seeded and minced | A tiny pinch, optional
[[table]] Black beans, rinsed and drained | 1 can (15 ounces), optional

[[steps]] Dress | Whisk lime, oil, salt, and pepper in a large bowl || Chop | Dice mango, cucumber, tomatoes, and onion || Toss | Fold everything into the dressing gently || Finish | Add avocado and herbs last || Serve | Eat within an hour for the best texture

Whisk the lime juice, olive oil, salt, and the smallest pinch of minced scotch bonnet in a large bowl, wearing gloves to cut the pepper. Add the mango, cucumber, tomatoes, and red onion, and toss gently so the fruit soaks up the dressing. If you are using black beans, stir them in now.

Dice the avocado last so it stays bright green, then fold it in carefully with the herbs so it does not turn to mash. Taste and add a little more lime or salt if needed. Serve it right away or within an hour, while the avocado is still fresh and firm.
### Tips, substitutions, and storage

Choose mangoes that give slightly when pressed and smell sweet near the stem, and avocados that yield to gentle pressure without feeling soft. If mangoes are out of season, ripe pineapple or papaya makes a lovely substitute. If you do not enjoy cilantro, use parsley, the more traditional Haitian herb, or a few chopped scallions.

This salad is best eaten the day it is made. To prepare ahead, chop the mango, cucumber, tomato, and onion and refrigerate them covered, then add the dressing and avocado just before serving. Leftovers keep for a day in the refrigerator, though the avocado will soften and darken a little.
![Bowl of fresh vegetable salad with sliced avocado](1564929360162-73cd686db4a1)
## Reflection questions

Take a quiet moment with these questions, on your own or with your family at the table. What foods from your own heritage already line up with God's original gift of plants, seeds, and fruit? Which one small change from this guide could you try this week without feeling overwhelmed? And how might you thank God for your body at each meal, not out of guilt but out of gratitude?
## A word of encouragement

Healthy eating is not a test you pass or fail, and God's love for you does not rise or fall with what is on your plate. Start where you are, with one more vegetable or one pot of brown rice. Let small faithful steps add up over time.

Above all, remember that the Bible invites us to enjoy the gifts God has given. As Paul wrote, "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). A colorful Haitian plate, shared with people you love, can be a beautiful act of worship.
## A prayer

Father, thank You for the food that grows from the earth and for the hands that prepare it. Thank You for our families, our heritage, and the tables where we gather. Help us to care for these bodies You have given us, not with fear but with joy and gratitude. Give us wisdom in our choices and grace when we fall short, and let every meal remind us that we belong to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
## Your next step

If you would like to explore what the Bible teaches about health, the Sabbath, and the abundant life Jesus offers, we would be glad to study with you. Request a free Bible study and go through these topics one on one, at your own pace, with someone who cares. And if you are near Alvarado, you are always welcome to join us on Saturday morning, when our church family shares a meal together after the Sabbath service.

posts.title: The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.seoTitle: How Much Sleep Do Adults Need? A Biblical View of Rest
posts.metaDesc: Most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep. Learn what the CDC and NIH say, what the Bible teaches about rest, and simple habits for sleeping better tonight.
posts.excerpt: Health experts say most adults need at least seven hours of sleep, and Scripture shows that receiving rest is an act of trust in the God who watches over us.
body: It is almost midnight, and the house is finally quiet. The dishes are done, the children are asleep, and you tell yourself you will rest right after a few more messages. Then the clock says one in the morning, your mind is still racing about tomorrow, and you wonder why you feel so tired all the time. If that sounds familiar, you are far from alone.

Many of us treat sleep as the first thing to cut when life gets full, and we quietly feel that going to bed early is a kind of laziness. Yet Scripture tells a different story. From the first week of Creation to the ministry of Jesus, the Bible presents rest not as weakness but as a gift from a loving Creator who knows exactly how we are made.

In this article we will look at what health experts say about how much sleep adults need, what the Bible teaches about sleep and trust, and why Seventh-day Adventists see caring for our bodies as part of our worship. Along the way you will find simple, practical habits for sleeping better tonight. This is general health education, not medical advice, so if you struggle with sleep often, please talk with your doctor.
## The short answer

[[stats]] 7 hours | Minimum nightly sleep the CDC recommends for adults 18 to 60 || 1 in 3 | US adults who report not getting enough rest or sleep every day (NHLBI) || 30 minutes | Wind down time before bed suggested by the Sleep Foundation

Most adults need at least seven hours of sleep each night. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends seven or more hours for adults ages 18 to 60, and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute notes that experts recommend between seven and nine hours a night for adults. Adults who regularly sleep fewer than seven hours may face more health problems than those who get enough.

Spiritually, the Bible invites us to see sleep as an act of trust. When we lie down and close our eyes, we admit that we cannot hold the world together by ourselves. God does not need us to stay awake in order to keep His promises, and He gives rest to His children as a gift. Sleep, received with gratitude, becomes a small daily surrender into His care.
## How much sleep do adults really need?

Sleep needs change across a lifetime. Children and teenagers need more sleep than adults, and older adults still need about seven to eight hours. The CDC publishes these ranges for each age group, a helpful guide for families setting bedtimes.
[[table]] Age group | Recommended sleep (CDC)
[[table]] School age, 6 to 12 years | 9 to 12 hours
[[table]] Teens, 13 to 17 years | 8 to 10 hours
[[table]] Adults, 18 to 60 years | 7 or more hours
[[table]] Adults, 61 to 64 years | 7 to 9 hours
[[table]] Adults, 65 and older | 7 to 8 hours

Those numbers can feel out of reach when you work long shifts, but the gap matters. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute reports that about one in three adults in the United States say they do not get enough rest or sleep every day. It also links ongoing sleep deficiency to heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, stroke, obesity, and depression, along with a higher risk of injury from accidents such as drowsy driving.

The CDC describes the other side of the picture as well. Getting enough sleep can help you get sick less often, stay at a healthy weight, lower your risk for serious conditions such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease, reduce stress, improve your mood, and sharpen your attention and memory. Sleep is not wasted time but the hidden work that makes the rest of your day possible.
## What the Bible says about sleep

The Bible does not give us a sleep schedule, and we should be careful not to read modern science into ancient texts. What Scripture does give us is a picture of God as the One who watches over us while we rest. It also offers a gentle correction for the anxious striving that keeps so many of us awake.
### Sleep as an act of trust

David wrote some of his most peaceful words during some of the most dangerous seasons of his life. Psalm 3 is titled as a psalm he wrote when he fled from his son Absalom, and yet he could say, "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me" (Psalm 3:5). In the very next psalm, he expresses the same quiet confidence.
> "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." Psalm 4:8, KJV

Notice where David places his safety. It is not in his own watchfulness or his plans for the next day, but in the Lord alone. When we lie awake replaying every worry, we are often carrying a weight God never asked us to carry through the night.
### The vanity of anxious overwork

Psalm 127 speaks directly to the habit of burning the candle at both ends. This psalm, whose title links it to Solomon, reminds us that unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Then he adds a striking line about sleep.
> "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Psalm 127:2, KJV

This verse does not condemn hard work, which Scripture honors in many places. It warns against the anxious, sorrowful toil that believes everything depends on us. The phrase "he giveth his beloved sleep" turns sleep into a love gift. God gives rest to the people He loves, and receiving that rest is one way of trusting His love.
## Elijah under the juniper tree

One of the most tender stories about rest in Scripture comes from the life of Elijah. After a dramatic victory on Mount Carmel, he received a death threat from Queen Jezebel and fled into the wilderness. Exhausted and discouraged, he sat under a juniper tree and asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4).
What God did next is beautiful. He did not lecture Elijah or tell him to pray harder. He let him sleep, and then He fed him.

> "And as he lay and slept under a juniper tree, behold, then an angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat. And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again." 1 Kings 19:5 to 6, KJV

The angel came a second time and said, "Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee" (1 Kings 19:7). Elijah then went in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God (1 Kings 19:8). Only after his body had been cared for did God speak to him in the still small voice. The order matters, and it is a gentle lesson for weary believers.
[[callout]] What God gave Elijah || Sleep, more than once || Simple food and water || A gentle touch, not a rebuke || Honest words about the journey ahead || Then, a quiet word from God Himself
![A softly lit table lamp beside a neatly made bed](1552858725-2758b5fb1286)
## Jesus invites tired disciples to rest

The same compassion shows up in the ministry of Jesus. After the disciples returned from a busy season of preaching and healing, crowds were pressing in from every side. Mark tells us they did not even have time to eat. Jesus noticed, and He made rest a priority.
> "And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat." Mark 6:31, KJV

Jesus did not see rest as a distraction from ministry but as part of faithful living. The Savior who said, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28), also knew that tired bodies need real sleep. If Jesus called His closest friends to rest, we can stop feeling guilty when our bodies ask for the same.
## Why Adventists see sleep as part of worship

Seventh-day Adventists believe that our bodies are a gift from God and that caring for them is part of how we honor Him. The church's Fundamental Belief 22, Christian Behavior, calls believers to live in harmony with biblical principles and includes adequate rest alongside exercise and a healthful diet. Paul put the principle simply: "whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). That includes how we sleep.

Many Adventist churches teach eight natural remedies for health: good nutrition, exercise, water, sunlight, temperance, fresh air, rest, and trust in God. Rest and trust sit side by side on that list for a reason. Most of us cannot truly rest until we trust, and sleep is often the first place where our faith or our fear shows up.

The weekly Sabbath carries this principle further. Fundamental Belief 20 describes it as "a day of delightful communion with God and one another" and "the day of rest, worship, and ministry," kept from sunset to sunset. Nightly sleep restores the body day by day, while the Sabbath restores the whole person week by week, a rhythm God built into creation.
[[link]] Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust | /blog/resting-in-his-presence-what-the-sabbath-teaches-us-about-trust/
## Practical ways to sleep better

Good intentions are not enough on their own, and most of us need a few simple habits that make sleep easier to receive. The suggestions below come from the CDC, Mayo Clinic, and the Sleep Foundation. None of them require special equipment.
### Keep a steady schedule

The CDC and Mayo Clinic both recommend going to bed and getting up at the same time each day, including weekends. A regular rhythm helps your body know when it is time to wind down. Mayo Clinic also suggests that if you cannot fall asleep within about 20 minutes, you get up and do something relaxing until you feel tired, rather than lying in bed frustrated.
### Prepare your room and your evening

Keep your bedroom quiet, dark, relaxing, and cool. The CDC advises turning off electronics at least 30 minutes before bed, and the Sleep Foundation suggests building in a 30 to 60 minute device free buffer before sleep, since screens keep the mind stimulated. It also recommends setting aside about 30 minutes to wind down with calming activities such as soft music, light stretching, or reading.
### Watch evening food, drink, and activity

The CDC recommends avoiding large meals and alcohol before bed and avoiding caffeine in the afternoon or evening. Adventists already avoid alcohol and many avoid caffeine altogether, and that choice can be a quiet blessing for sleep. Daytime activity helps too, since the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans note that it can improve sleep quality, and Mayo Clinic suggests avoiding being active too close to bedtime.
### Lay your worries down before you lie down

Mayo Clinic recommends settling concerns before bed, for example by writing them down and setting them aside for tomorrow. For a believer, that list can become a prayer. Writing down what weighs on you and placing it before God is a practical way to obey Peter's counsel to cast all your care upon Him, because He cares for you (1 Peter 5:7).

[[steps]] Set a bedtime | Choose a time that allows at least seven hours || Screens off | Put devices away 30 to 60 minutes before bed || Dim the room | Keep it quiet, dark, and cool || Pray your worries | Write them down and give them to God || Read and rest | Close with a psalm, then lights out
### Know when to see a doctor

An occasional sleepless night is normal. If trouble sleeping happens often, though, Mayo Clinic advises contacting your health care provider so that any underlying cause can be found and treated. The NHLBI notes that an estimated 50 to 70 million Americans have chronic sleep disorders, so asking for help is common and wise. Seeing a doctor about sleep is not a lack of faith. It is good stewardship of the body God gave you.
![A night sky filled with stars](1628498188904-036f5e25e93e)
## A word for families and busy households

In many Haitian homes, evenings are full and lively, with food to prepare, family calling from Haiti, and homework to check. Yet children and teens need even more sleep than adults, so a household rhythm that protects bedtime is one of the kindest gifts parents can give. A short family worship with a song in Kreyòl or English, a psalm, and a prayer can signal that the day is closing. It also teaches children that we fall asleep in the care of a God who never sleeps, because "he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4).
## Reflection questions

Take a quiet moment with these questions tonight, perhaps before you turn off the light. What is one habit that regularly keeps you up later than you intend, and what would it look like to hand that time back to God? When you lie awake worrying, what would change if you truly believed that God keeps watch while you sleep? How might your family protect bedtime as a gift instead of treating it as something to squeeze in when everything else is done?
## A word of encouragement

If you have been running on empty, hear this gently: you are not a failure for being tired. Elijah was tired, the disciples were tired, and God met them with food, sleep, and kindness before He gave them their next assignment. He is the same God today, and He knows your frame and remembers that you are dust (Psalm 103:14).

Start small by choosing one habit from this article and trying it for a week. Go to bed a little earlier or pray through your worries on paper. Each time you lie down in peace, you are telling God that you trust Him, and that simple act of trust is a beautiful form of worship.
## A prayer

Father, thank You for the gift of sleep and for watching over me through every night. Forgive me for the times I have carried burdens You never asked me to carry. Teach me to lie down in peace and to trust You with tomorrow. Restore my body, quiet my mind, and let my rest bring glory to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
## Your next step

If worry or weariness has been keeping you awake, you do not have to carry it alone. Our church family would be honored to pray with you, so share a prayer request below. We also gather for prayer meeting every Wednesday at 7:30 PM at 205 E Carver St in Alvarado, Texas, and you are always welcome.

posts.metaDesc: Make a hearty plant based soup joumou with squash, vegetables, pasta, epis, and chickpeas, and learn the 1804 freedom story and UNESCO recognition behind it.
posts.excerpt: The story of Haiti's freedom soup, from January 1, 1804 to UNESCO recognition, with a full plant based soup joumou recipe the whole table can share.
body: It is the last night of December, and somewhere a Haitian kitchen is already busy. The squash has been peeled and cubed, the epis is waiting in a jar, and a big pot is being pulled down from the top shelf because this soup is never made in small amounts. By morning, bowls will be passed to family, neighbors, and anyone who walks through the door. For many Haitians at home and around the world, the new year does not truly begin until the first spoonful of soup joumou.

Maybe you grew up with that tradition and want to keep it alive in a new country. Maybe you are married into a Haitian family and want to learn the soup your in laws talk about every January. Or maybe you follow a plant based diet and wonder whether a dish usually made with beef can still taste like celebration. Whatever brought you here, this soup is worth learning, because it carries a story of freedom that every one of us can understand.

In this article we will look at the history behind soup joumou, why UNESCO recognized it as part of the world's cultural heritage, and what the Bible says about the freedom it celebrates. Then we will walk through a full plant based soup joumou recipe, rich with squash, vegetables, pasta, and epis, with chickpeas standing in for the beef so the whole table can share one pot.
## The short answer

Soup joumou is a Haitian squash soup traditionally eaten on January 1, Haiti's Independence Day. Under French colonial rule it was reserved for slave owners, and after Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804, Haitians claimed the soup as their own and made it a symbol of freedom and dignity. In 2021, UNESCO added it to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
[[stats]] 1804 | Year Haiti declared independence on January 1 || 2021 | Year UNESCO inscribed joumou soup || 8 | Generous servings from one pot

A plant based version keeps everything that makes the soup special, the bright orange squash broth, the tender vegetables, the pasta, and the herb filled epis, while swapping the beef for chickpeas. The result is hearty, colorful, and fully in keeping with the Adventist health message, which encourages a balanced vegetarian diet with legumes, whole grains, fruits, and vegetables.

Chickpeas are a smart stand in for beef. Harvard's Nutrition Source describes legumes as a source of protein and both soluble and insoluble fiber, and notes that whole legumes are naturally low in saturated fat and sodium. They also hold their shape in a long simmer, so every spoonful gets a little something to bite into.
## The history of soup joumou
### A soup that was forbidden

During the colonial period, the land we now call Haiti was the French colony of Saint Domingue, and enslaved Africans did the brutal work of its plantations. According to UNESCO, joumou soup was originally reserved for slave owners. Al Jazeera's report on the UNESCO decision explains that enslaved Haitians prepared the soup but were never allowed to eat it themselves.
Think about what that means. People spent hours cutting, stirring, and seasoning a meal they could smell but never taste. The soup became a daily reminder of who was considered free and who was not.
### January 1, 1804

On January 1, 1804, in the port city of Gonaïves, Jean Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the independence of Haiti. Haiti became the first nation in Latin America and the Caribbean to win its independence, and the second in the Americas after the United States. It was also the first country to be founded by formerly enslaved people.

Haitians celebrated their freedom by eating the very soup that had been denied to them. What had been a symbol of exclusion became a symbol of liberty. To this day, soup joumou is eaten on New Year's Day to remember the revolution, and many families continue serving it on January 2, Ancestry Day, a holiday honoring the heroes of independence.
[[time]] Colonial era | A soup for slave owners | Enslaved people grow and cook the squash but are not allowed to eat the soup.
[[time]] January 1, 1804 | Independence in Gonaïves | Dessalines proclaims Haiti free, and Haitians claim the soup as their own.
[[time]] Every January 1 | The first meal of the year | Families share soup joumou to remember freedom and dignity.
[[time]] December 2021 | Recognized by UNESCO | Joumou soup is added to the Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
### Recognized by the world

In December 2021, UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage committee inscribed joumou soup on its Representative List. It was Haiti's first inscription on the list. UNESCO describes the soup as a celebratory dish tied to Haitian identity, one that promotes social cohesion and a sense of belonging, and that became a symbol of the dignity and resilience of Haitians after independence.

UNESCO also notes that the soup is a traditional Sunday breakfast, not only a New Year's dish. The traditional ingredients it lists include giraumon pumpkin, vegetables, plantains, meat, pasta, and spices. Recipes vary from family to family, and every Haitian kitchen seems to have its own small secret.
![Bowl of golden pumpkin soup with bread and whole pumpkins](1764015939164-d5359a90c79c)
## Freedom through the eyes of Scripture

The story of soup joumou echoes one of the oldest themes in the Bible. God revealed Himself to Israel as the One who brought them out of slavery in Egypt, and He gave them a weekly Sabbath in part to remember that freedom (Deuteronomy 5:15). Slaves never rest. Free people do.

The New Testament carries that theme even deeper. Jesus told the people listening to Him, "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" (John 8:36). He was speaking about a freedom no government can grant and no chain can take away, freedom from sin, guilt, and fear.
> "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage." Galatians 5:1, KJV

Paul wrote these words to Christians who were tempted to trade the grace of Jesus for a life of trying to earn God's favor. His message was simple: you have been set free, so do not go back. A bowl of soup joumou can become a small sermon at the table, reminding us that the God who cares about justice for the oppressed also offers every person freedom through Jesus.

The psalmist adds an invitation that fits a festive meal perfectly: "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him" (Psalm 34:8). The verse is about experiencing God's goodness personally, not about food, but there is something fitting about tasting a dish of freedom and remembering the One who sets us free.
[[link]] Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust | /blog/resting-in-his-presence-what-the-sabbath-teaches-us-about-trust/
## Plant based soup joumou recipe

This recipe makes about 8 generous servings, enough for a family gathering or a week of lunches. Plan on about 30 minutes of prep and about 1 hour and 15 minutes of cooking. Kabocha, calabaza, or butternut squash all work well, and the soup gets its body from the puréed squash, so there is no need for cream or butter.
[[table]] Ingredient | Amount
[[table]] Kabocha, calabaza, or butternut squash, peeled and cubed | 3 pounds (about 8 cups)
[[table]] Water or low sodium vegetable broth | 10 cups, divided
[[table]] Olive oil | 2 tablespoons
[[table]] Haitian epis | 1/2 cup
[[table]] Yellow onion, chopped | 1 large
[[table]] Garlic, minced | 4 cloves
[[table]] Celery, sliced | 2 stalks
[[table]] Leek, white and light green parts, sliced | 1 medium
[[table]] Carrots, sliced into rounds | 3 medium
[[table]] Potatoes, peeled and cubed | 2 medium
[[table]] Turnip or malanga, peeled and cubed | 1 medium
[[table]] Green cabbage, thinly sliced | 1/2 small head (about 4 cups)
[[table]] Cooked chickpeas, rinsed | 3 cups (or two 15 ounce cans)
[[table]] Tomato paste | 2 tablespoons
[[table]] Fresh thyme | 6 sprigs
[[table]] Fresh parsley, chopped | 1/2 cup
[[table]] Whole cloves | 3
[[table]] Whole scotch bonnet pepper | 1, left whole
[[table]] Rigatoni, penne, or spaghetti broken into pieces | 8 ounces

[[table]] Salt and black pepper | To taste

[[steps]] Squash | Simmer cubed squash until very soft || Purée | Blend squash with its cooking water until smooth || Base | Sauté epis, onion, garlic, and tomato paste || Simmer | Add broth, vegetables, chickpeas, and herbs || Finish | Add pasta and cabbage, then lime and salt
### Step 1: Cook and purée the squash

Place the cubed squash in a large pot with 4 cups of the water or broth. Bring it to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer, covered, for about 20 to 25 minutes, until a fork slides through the squash with no resistance. Carefully blend the squash and its cooking liquid until completely smooth, using a blender in batches or an immersion blender right in the pot. For the silkiest texture, press the purée through a fine strainer, as some Haitian cooks do.
### Step 2: Build the flavor base

In a large soup pot, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the epis, onion, garlic, celery, and leek, and cook for about 5 minutes, stirring often, until fragrant and soft. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for another minute or two so it darkens slightly and loses its raw taste.
### Step 3: Simmer the vegetables and chickpeas

Pour the squash purée into the pot along with the remaining 6 cups of water or broth. Add the carrots, potatoes, turnip or malanga, chickpeas, thyme, cloves, and the whole scotch bonnet pepper. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for about 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the potatoes and carrots are tender. Keep the pepper whole so it adds flavor and gentle warmth without making the soup too spicy, and remove it before serving.
### Step 4: Add the cabbage and pasta

Stir in the cabbage and the pasta and simmer for another 12 to 15 minutes, until the pasta is tender and the cabbage is soft. If the soup becomes too thick, add hot water a half cup at a time. Remove the thyme stems, the cloves if you can find them, and the scotch bonnet. Stir in the parsley and lime juice, then taste and season with salt and black pepper.
![Fresh carrots and leeks piled together at a market stall](1471193945509-9ad0617afabf)
## Tips, substitutions, and storage

The quality of your squash makes the biggest difference. A deeply orange kabocha or calabaza gives a richer color and sweeter flavor than a pale squash. If your epis already contains salt or bouillon, add salt slowly at the end so the soup does not become too salty. Choose a low sodium broth whenever you can, because soups can carry a lot of hidden salt.

For extra protein, you can add white beans along with the chickpeas, and for a gluten free version use a gluten free pasta and cook it separately so it does not break apart. Plantain or yam can replace the potatoes for a more traditional touch. If you do not have epis on hand, blend a handful of parsley, a few scallions, a green bell pepper, garlic, thyme leaves, a little oil, and a squeeze of lime, and you will have a simple version in minutes.

[[callout]] Make ahead tips || Cook and purée the squash a day early || Keep pasta separate if storing leftovers || Add a splash of water when reheating || Freeze the soup without pasta for best texture

The pasta keeps absorbing broth as it sits, so if you plan to have leftovers, cook the pasta separately and add it to each bowl. FoodSafety.gov advises that vegetable soups and stews keep for 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator and 2 to 3 months in the freezer, and that leftovers should be reheated to 165°F. The soup often tastes even better the next day, which makes it a wonderful dish to cook on Friday for the Sabbath.
## Reflection questions

Spend a few minutes with these questions, perhaps while the soup simmers or around the table with your family. What does freedom mean to you, both the freedom our ancestors fought for and the freedom Jesus offers? Is there an area of your life where you still feel bound, and what would it look like to bring it to Christ? And how could you use a family tradition like soup joumou to tell the next generation about God's faithfulness?
## A word of encouragement

The story of soup joumou reminds us that what was once used to divide people can become a gift that brings them together. That is the story of the gospel too. Jesus takes what was broken and turns it into something that tells of His grace.

Whether this is your hundredth pot of soup joumou or your very first, cook it with gratitude. Share it with someone who needs a warm meal or a kind word. And as you taste it, remember that the freedom Christ gives is for every person at the table.
## A prayer

Lord, thank You for the gift of freedom and for the courage of those who came before us. Thank You most of all for Jesus, who sets us free indeed. As we gather around the table, help us remember Your faithfulness and share Your love with everyone we meet. Break every chain that still holds us, and teach us to stand fast in the liberty You give. In Jesus' name, Amen.
## Your next step

If the story of freedom in this soup has stirred something in your heart, we would love to share more with you. Request a free Bible study and explore what Scripture teaches about the freedom Jesus offers, one on one, at your own pace. You are also warmly welcome to worship with us on Saturday morning in Alvarado, where we gather in Kreyòl and English and share a meal together after the Sabbath service.

posts.title: When Prayer Feels Quiet
posts.author: Elder Guy Jean-Louis
posts.seoTitle: Why Does God Not Answer My Prayers? When God Feels Silent
posts.metaDesc: When prayer feels unanswered, Scripture offers hope. Learn from Hannah, David, Elijah, and Daniel, and what Jesus taught about praying without giving up.
posts.excerpt: When prayer feels unanswered, the stories of Hannah, David, Elijah, and Daniel remind us that God's silence is not His absence and that He hears us from the very first day.
body: You have prayed about it for months, maybe for years, in the morning and again late at night. Still the diagnosis is the same, the job has not come, the relationship is still broken, and heaven seems strangely quiet. Somewhere along the way, a hard question has started to form in your heart: is God even listening to me?

If you have ever felt that way, you are in good company. Some of the most faithful people in the Bible prayed through long seasons of silence, weeping, questioning, and sometimes wanting to give up. God made sure their stories were written down, so that we would know we are not alone when prayer feels quiet.

In this article we will walk through the stories of Hannah, David, Elijah, and Daniel, and listen to what Jesus taught about praying without giving up. Our hope is not to offer easy answers. It is to help you keep talking to a God who has not stopped loving you, even when you cannot hear Him.
## The short answer
[[stats]] 21 days | Daniel waited before the angel arrived || 4 times | David asks "how long" in Psalm 13 || Always | Jesus said to pray and not to faint

The Bible never promises that every prayer will be answered quickly or in the way we hope. What it does promise is that God hears His children, that He is working even when we cannot see it, and that silence is not the same as absence. Sometimes God says yes, sometimes He says no, and sometimes He says wait. The quiet seasons of prayer are often where trust grows deepest.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church's page on prayer is honest about this. It calls the times when God seems not to answer one of the hardest parts of prayer, and reminds us that His timing differs from ours. It describes God not as a vending machine but as a loving Father who builds character in every season.
## Why does God sometimes seem silent?

Many articles on this question focus mainly on what the person praying might be doing wrong. Scripture does teach that wrong motives (James 4:3), cherished sin, or broken relationships at home (1 Peter 3:7) can hinder prayer, and those are worth examining humbly. But it would be unbiblical to suggest that every quiet season is caused by something you did wrong.

The Bible points to other reasons too. "To every thing there is a season" (Ecclesiastes 3:1), and God may be answering in a way we do not yet recognize. Sometimes His answer is no, because like a good parent He knows what we ask would not be good for us. Jesus said, "your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him" (Matthew 6:8).

Scripture also pulls back the curtain on something we rarely consider: there is a real spiritual conflict happening beyond what we can see. The Seventh-day Adventist Church describes this in Fundamental Belief 8, The Great Controversy, as a cosmic conflict between Christ and Satan in which all of humanity is caught up. We will see that conflict clearly in the story of Daniel.

[[callout]] What silence does not mean || It does not mean God has stopped loving you (Jeremiah 31:3) || It does not mean your prayer was not heard (Daniel 10:12) || It does not mean you lack enough faith to be heard || It does not mean the story is over
## Hannah: pouring out a sorrowful heart

Hannah longed for a child, while her husband's other wife Peninnah had children and "provoked her sore, for to make her fret" (1 Samuel 1:6). This went on "year by year," and Hannah "wept, and did not eat" (1 Samuel 1:7). Her prayer was not one request answered the next morning but a sorrow she carried for years.
> "And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." 1 Samuel 1:10, KJV

Hannah prayed so intensely that the priest Eli thought she was drunk. Her reply is one of the most honest descriptions of prayer in the Bible: "I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:15). She did not dress up her pain in polite words.

Something changed in Hannah before anything changed in her circumstances. She "went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad" (1 Samuel 1:18). Later she bore a son and named him Samuel, "Because I have asked him of the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:20). Her story shows that peace can come through prayer even while we still wait for the answer.
## David: asking "how long?"
Psalm 13 holds one of the most honest prayers in Scripture. David does not open with praise or polished language. He opens with a complaint many tired believers will recognize.

> "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" Psalm 13:1 to 2, KJV

Four times in two verses David asks "how long." He feels forgotten and tired of carrying sorrow every day, yet God chose to include this prayer in His Word. That tells us something important. Honest lament is not a lack of faith; it is a form of faith, because it keeps talking to God instead of walking away.

Then, with no sign that his situation has changed, David turns: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation" (Psalm 13:5). His trust comes not from a sudden answer but from remembering who God is. When prayer feels quiet, we can follow the same path from honest questions to a decision to trust.
![Sunlight streaming through a window into a quiet, empty room](1748908271645-1d2b72291839)
## Elijah: when you are too tired to go on

Elijah had just seen a great victory on Mount Carmel, yet soon after, threatened by Queen Jezebel, he ran for his life. Exhausted and afraid, he sat under a juniper tree and prayed, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers" (1 Kings 19:4). Even great faith can run out of strength.

God's first response was not a lecture but care. An angel touched Elijah and said, "Arise and eat" (1 Kings 19:5), and later came again, "because the journey is too great for thee" (1 Kings 19:7). Sometimes the most spiritual thing we can do in a dark season is to rest, eat, and let God care for our bodies before we try to understand everything.

At Mount Horeb, a great wind came, then an earthquake, then a fire, "but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice" (1 Kings 19:12). Elijah also believed he was alone, but God told him of "seven thousand in Israel" who had remained faithful (1 Kings 19:18). God may be speaking more gently than we expect, and we may be less alone than we feel.
[[link]] The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship | /blog/the-gift-of-rest-why-sleep-is-part-of-our-worship/
## Daniel: heard from the first day

Daniel's story may offer the most surprising window into unanswered prayer. In Daniel 10, the prophet spent "three full weeks" mourning and fasting, eating "no pleasant bread" as he sought God for understanding (Daniel 10:2 to 3). For twenty one days, there seemed to be no response.

> "Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words. But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me." Daniel 10:12 to 13, KJV

Daniel's prayer was heard on the very first day, and the delay was not God ignoring him. A real conflict was taking place in the unseen realm, and the messenger was withstood until Michael came to help. Adventists see here a glimpse of the great controversy, and many Adventist teachers identify Michael with Christ Himself.

We should not build more on this passage than it says, since the Bible does not tell us every delay has the same cause. But it does show clearly that a quiet heaven is not an inactive heaven. While Daniel waited, God was already moving, and the same may be true for you.
[[time]] Years | Hannah | She weeps and prays year after year before Samuel is born (1 Samuel 1:7 to 20).
[[time]] Daily sorrow | David | He asks "how long" and chooses to trust God's mercy (Psalm 13).
[[time]] Forty days | Elijah | Strengthened by food and rest, he travels to Horeb and hears a still small voice (1 Kings 19:8 to 12).
[[time]] Twenty one days | Daniel | His prayer is heard on the first day, while the answer is delayed by unseen conflict (Daniel 10:12 to 13).
## Jesus: pray and do not faint
Jesus knew His followers would face seasons when prayer felt unanswered, so He told a story for them. Luke states its purpose before the story begins. It is a word for every weary heart.
> "And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint." Luke 18:1, KJV

In the parable, a widow keeps asking an unjust judge for justice, and he finally helps her simply because she will not stop (Luke 18:2 to 5). Then Jesus draws the contrast: "And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily" (Luke 18:7 to 8).

The point is that God is the opposite of the unjust judge. If an uncaring judge responds to persistence, how much more will a loving Father. Jesus ends by asking, "when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" (Luke 18:8).

Jesus Himself prayed, "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt" (Matthew 26:39). The cup did not pass, and through His suffering came our salvation. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed and heard, "My grace is sufficient for thee" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Sometimes the answer is not a change in our circumstances but God's strength within them.
## How to keep praying when God feels silent
In a quiet season we also need practical ways to keep going. These steps are not a formula for answers. They simply keep the conversation with God open while you wait.

[[steps]] Be honest | Tell God exactly how you feel, as Hannah and David did || Care for yourself | Rest, eat, and let God restore you, as He did for Elijah || Remember | Write down past times God has been faithful || Keep asking | Follow Jesus' call to pray and not faint || Do not wait alone | Share the burden with others who can pray with you

When your own words run dry, pray the Psalms, such as "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation" (Psalm 62:1). When you do not know what to say, remember that "the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered" (Romans 8:26). Even a sigh can be a prayer.

It also helps not to carry the weight alone. At Shekinah in Alvarado, the church family gathers for prayer meeting on Wednesdays at 7:30 PM, and you can send a private prayer request through our website. When we cannot pray, others can hold us up until our voice returns.
![Misty mountains rising above a quiet forest in the morning](1516118942927-391ce247e733)
## Reflection questions

Take some time with these questions, perhaps with a journal open. Which of these Bible stories feels closest to what you are experiencing right now, and why? What would it look like for you to pour out your heart honestly to God this week, without trying to sound strong? And what is one past answer to prayer you can write down and return to when the silence feels long?
## A word of encouragement

If prayer feels quiet for you today, please do not stop talking to God. Hannah was given peace before she was given a son, and David questioned and then chose to sing. Elijah was fed and rested before he heard the still small voice. Daniel was heard on the very first day, though he did not know it for three weeks.

You may not understand what God is doing right now, and that is all right, because faith only asks that we keep turning toward the One who loves us. "Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning" (Psalm 30:5). Hold on to Him, and let Him hold on to you.
## A prayer

Father, sometimes my prayers feel like they disappear into the quiet. You know how long I have been asking, and You know how tired my heart is. Thank You that You heard me from the first day, even when I could not hear You. Give me the honesty of Hannah, the trust of David, the rest You gave Elijah, and the patience of Daniel. Help me keep praying and not lose heart, and let Your peace guard my heart while I wait. In Jesus' name, Amen.
## Your next step

You do not have to carry this alone. If something heavy is on your heart, send us a prayer request, and our church family will pray with you and for you. Share as much or as little as you like, and your request will be handled with care.

posts.title: Walk With Me: Starting a Sabbath Afternoon Walking Group
posts.author: Health Ministries
posts.seoTitle: Benefits of Walking and Starting a Sabbath Walking Group
posts.metaDesc: See the health benefits of walking, how many minutes adults need each week, and how to start a simple Sabbath afternoon walk with family, friends, or church.
posts.excerpt: Walking is one of the simplest ways to care for the body God gave you, and a gentle Sabbath afternoon walk with others can turn exercise into fellowship and worship.
body: The Sabbath meal is finished, the plates are stacked, and the afternoon stretches out ahead like an open field. Some of the family are drifting toward the couch, the children are getting restless, and someone suggests a nap. Then another voice says, "Why don't we go for a walk?" It is such a simple idea, and yet that one question can turn a sleepy afternoon into one of the sweetest hours of the week.

Walking is the kind of exercise almost anyone can start. It needs no gym membership, no special skill, and very little equipment beyond a comfortable pair of shoes. When you walk with others, it becomes something more than exercise. It becomes conversation, friendship, and, on the Sabbath, a quiet way to enjoy the world God made.

This guide covers what health experts say about the benefits of walking and how much activity adults need. It also looks at what the Bible says about walking and nature on the Sabbath, and how a family, a group of friends, or a small church group can start a Sabbath afternoon walk. It is general health education, so if you have a medical condition or have not been active for a while, please check with your doctor before you begin.
## The short answer

[[stats]] 150 minutes | Weekly moderate activity the CDC recommends for adults || 30 minutes | One way to get there: 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week || 60 minutes | Daily activity youth ages 6 to 17 need (HHS)

The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity each week, and it names brisk walking as an example of moderate activity. You do not have to do it all at once. The CDC suggests that 30 minutes a day on five days a week is one simple way to reach the goal, and some physical activity is better than none.

Spiritually, a Sabbath afternoon walk fits beautifully with the purpose of the day. Jesus walked through fields with His disciples on the Sabbath, and Scripture invites us to see God's glory in creation. A gentle walk together, with conversation and gratitude, can be a restful way to honor the Lord of the Sabbath rather than a break from Him.
## The benefits of walking

Health organizations agree that walking is one of the most accessible forms of exercise there is. Mayo Clinic lists a wide range of benefits that come from regular walking. It can help you maintain a healthy weight, prevent or manage conditions such as heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers, improve heart health and endurance, and strengthen bones and muscles.

Mayo Clinic also notes that walking can boost energy, improve mood, thinking, memory, and sleep, and reduce stress and anxiety. For older adults, it can improve physical function and lower the risk of falls. The American Heart Association likewise says walking can have a significant impact on your health by lowering your chances of heart disease. The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans add that some benefits come right away, since physical activity has immediate benefits such as reducing anxiety and blood pressure and improving the quality of sleep.

[[callout]] What regular walking can do || Support a healthy weight || Lower the risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes || Strengthen bones and muscles || Lift mood and reduce stress || Improve sleep and energy || Help older adults lower fall risk

The guidelines also make a point that encourages beginners. The first key guideline for adults is simply to move more and sit less, and any amount of physical activity has some health benefits. If you have not exercised in years, you do not need to start at 150 minutes. A short walk after lunch counts, and so does every step you add from there.
## How much walking do you need?

The federal Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommend that adults get at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate intensity aerobic activity each week. The CDC adds that adults also benefit from muscle strengthening activity on at least two days a week. For children and teens, the guidelines call for at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity every day for ages 6 through 17.
